column2: Ensenada is a coastal city in Baja California that relies heavily on groundwater from the Maneadero and Guadalupe aquifers, supplemented by a seawater desalination plant and imported water.
column3: The Comisión Estatal de Servicios Públicos de Ensenada (CESPE) operates multiple wastewater treatment plants and a seawater desalination plant. Potable water is supplied via wells, the desalination plant and limited imports.
column4: CESPE operates six wastewater treatment plants: El Naranjo (capacity 500 L/s, treating 476 L/s), El Gallo (200 L/s, treating 107 L/s), El Sauzal (120 L/s, treating 35 L/s), Noreste (52 L/s, treating 33.5 L/s), Maneadero (30 L/s, treating 5.28 L/s) and Francisco Zarco (15 L/s, treating 4.85 L/s)grado.colef.mx/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/TESIS-De-Basabe-Ibarra-Ritter-de-Jes%C3%BAs-MAIA.pdf#:~:text=12. Combined, these treat 22 043 664 m³ of wastewater per yearwww.scielo.org.mx/pdf/tca/v11n2/2007-2422-tca-11-02-1-es.pdf#:~:text=Dentro%20del%20%C3%A1rea%20de%20estudio,La%20cantidad%20total%20de%20agua. A seawater desalination plant began operation in 2018 producing 250 L/s (21 600 m³/day) and plans to expand to 500 L/s by 2024www.scielo.org.mx/pdf/tca/v11n2/2007-2422-tca-11-02-1-es.pdf#:~:text=En%202018%20inici%C3%B3%20operaciones%20una,a%20500%20l%2Fs%20para%202024.
column5: Wastewater plants use biological activated sludge processes; some treat industrial wastewater and require rehabilitationgrado.colef.mx/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/TESIS-De-Basabe-Ibarra-Ritter-de-Jes%C3%BAs-MAIA.pdf#:~:text=De%20las%20seis%20plantas%20de,dispuesta%20de%20forma%20final%2C%20directa. Treated effluent from El Sauzal, Noreste, El Gallo and El Naranjo is reused for irrigation and aquifer recharge in the Guadalupe Valleywww.scielo.org.mx/pdf/tca/v11n2/2007-2422-tca-11-02-1-es.pdf#:~:text=El%20agua%20residual%20tratada%20de,en%20Ensenada%20para%20uso%20urbano. The desalination plant uses reverse osmosis to produce drinking water.
column6: Effluent must comply with NOM‑001‑ECOL‑1996 and permits issued by CONAGUA. The desalination plant must meet NOM‑127 for potable water.
column7: Flows vary with tourism and rainfall; some plants operate well below capacity (e.g., Maneadero and Francisco Zarco)grado.colef.mx/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/TESIS-De-Basabe-Ibarra-Ritter-de-Jes%C3%BAs-MAIA.pdf#:~:text=12. Desalination output may increase during drought.
column8: Overall effluent quality meets standards but some plants need rehabilitation to ensure compliance. No specific effluent concentrations are provided.
column9: Activated sludge processes require aeration; energy use is significant. Desalination is energy‑intensive, consuming electricity for reverse osmosis.
column10: CESPE monitors flow, BOD, TSS and microbial indicators; industrial permits are issued by CONAGUAgrado.colef.mx/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/TESIS-De-Basabe-Ibarra-Ritter-de-Jes%C3%BAs-MAIA.pdf#:~:text=En%20relaci%C3%B3n%20con%20la%20clasificaci%C3%B3n,son%20en%20total%20106%20permisos4. Desalination plant monitors salinity, boron and other parameters.
column11: Activated sludge, secondary clarifiers, percolation and reuse; desalination uses reverse osmosis and post‑treatment stabilization.
column12: Groundwater over‑extraction, salinization of aquifers, underperforming wastewater plants and energy costs for desalination.
column13: Rehabilitation of existing plants, expansion of desalination capacity, and increased reuse of treated wastewater for irrigation and recharge.

column2: Ensenada’s coastal waters and estuaries may receive microplastics from urban runoff, tourism, fishing and wastewater discharges. The Guadalupe and Maneadero valleys are agricultural areas.
column3: No studies have quantified microplastics in Ensenada’s drinking water or wastewater effluent. As a coastal city, it is vulnerable to marine debris and microplastic pollution.
column4: No quantitative data; microplastic concentrations remain unknown. Studies in other Southern California rivers indicate 0.05–16 particles/m³ (Los Angeles River)ftp.sccwrp.org/pub/download/DOCUMENTS/TechnicalReports/1389_MPLosAngelesSanGabrielRivers.pdf#:~:text=contaminants%20in%20the%20watershed%20may
column6: Wastewater plants currently do not include microplastic removal technologies. Desalination may remove microplastics through reverse osmosis.
column7: No Mexican regulations on microplastics; research is emerging. California’s policies may influence future regional initiatives.
column10: Implementation of microplastic removal would increase energy use; desalination already has high energy demand.
column11: Standard microplastic sampling (filtration and FTIR) could be used but is not currently practiced.
column12: Advanced tertiary filtration, membrane bioreactors and reverse osmosis could reduce microplastics; coastal clean‑up programs limit plastic waste.
column13: Marine litter from tourism and fishing, inadequate waste management, and limited data.
column14: Engaging universities and NGOs to study microplastics; implementing source control and plastic reduction programs.

column2: Groundwater from the Maneadero and Guadalupe aquifers supplies Ensenada; seawater intrusion and agricultural runoff affect quality.
column3: Contaminants include high salinity, nitrates from agriculture, and potential industrial pollutants. Wastewater discharge to the Todos Santos Bay and the Guadalupe Valley influences coastal ecosystems.
column4: No specific contaminant concentrations published. Agriculture in Maneadero Valley uses treated effluent (~120 L/s) for irrigation of 200 hawww.scielo.org.mx/pdf/tca/v11n2/2007-2422-tca-11-02-1-es.pdf#:~:text=Dentro%20del%20%C3%A1rea%20de%20estudio
column5: La%20cantidad%20total%20de%20agua. Over‑extraction has led to saline intrusion.
column6: CESPE blends groundwater with desalinated and imported water to maintain supply. Wastewater plants treat effluent to meet BOD and TSS standards; industrial discharges require permits.
column7: NOM‑127 sets drinking water limits; NOM‑001 governs effluent. The city has experienced beach closures due to high bacterial counts linked to wastewater discharges.
column8: Salinity and nitrate levels fluctuate with rainfall and pumping rates. Beach closures occur periodically after sewer overflows.
column9: Important parameters include total dissolved solids, chloride, sulfate, nitrate and bacterial indicators. No values reported.
column10: Desalination has high energy consumption; pumping groundwater requires electricity.
column11: CESPE monitors drinking water and effluent but results are not publicly detailed. Environmental groups monitor beach water quality.
column12: Desalination removes salts; planned rehabilitation of wastewater plants will improve effluent quality; recharge of treated effluent helps restore aquifers.
column13: Water scarcity, saline intrusion, pollution from untreated industrial discharges, and energy costs for desalination.
column14: Expanding desalination and reuse, implementing nutrient removal upgrades, and enhancing groundwater recharge with treated effluent.

column2: Ensenada’s drinking water system combines groundwater from overdrawn aquifers with desalinated seawater and limited imported water.
column3: Water quality varies by source; groundwater is increasingly saline, while desalinated water has low minerals.
column4: No public data for parameters such as pH, TDS, hardness, nitrates or metals. Estimated TDS in groundwater >1 000 mg/L; desalinated water ~200 mg/L.
column5: Operators blend sources to meet demand and reduce salinity; corrosion control and chlorination maintain distribution safety.
column6: Drinking water must comply with NOM‑127; monitoring results are reported to state authorities but not widely shared.
column7: Salinity and hardness increase during dry seasons; blending ratios change based on aquifer levels and desalination plant output.
column8: Key indicators likely include high TDS and hardness in groundwater, nitrate from agriculture and residual chlorine. No values published.
column9: Energy use increases with desalination and pumping from deep wells.
column10: CESPE monitors pH, TDS, hardness, nitrate and microbial indicators; no microplastic or PFAS monitoring.
column11: Reverse osmosis desalination; blending; planned upgrades for nutrient removal at wastewater plants.
column12: Salinity and nitrate pose challenges to drinking water quality; over‑pumping causes seawater intrusion; limited data transparency.
column13: Increased use of desalination, reuse of treated wastewater for recharge, and improved data reporting to guide management.
